title: Forced-Labor Tariffs Replace Expiring Levy as Trump Rebuilds Trade Wall, Oil Crosses $100 on Houthi Red Sea Blockade
subhead: Trump's new forced-labor tariffs on 60 countries took effect just as the 10% global duty expired, while Brent crude topped $100 after Houthis struck Saudi tankers — creating a second chokepoint alongside the Strait of Hormuz closure and pushing Fed hike odds past one-in-three ahead of next week's meeting.

sections.heading: Forced-Labor Tariffs Replace Expired 10% Duty, Covering 99.4% of Imports
sections.body:
The Trump administration imposed new tariffs of 10% and 12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners — including the EU, China, Japan, South Korea, Canada, India, and the UK — effective at 12:01 a.m. EDT on Friday, the exact moment the temporary 10% global tariff expired after 150 days. The move is the first step in rebuilding Trump's tariff wall after the Supreme Court struck down his 'reciprocal' duties in February.

The new duties, imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, allege that trading partners failed to curb forced-labor imports in their supply chains — a justification that drew pushback from virtually every targeted country. Australia and Brazil called the tariffs unjustified; Norway said there was 'no basis' for them. The EU noted that the tariffs stayed within the caps agreed in the EU-US Joint Statement, while the UK said the deal meant zero tariffs on whisky and medical technology. China's effective rate moves back toward the 20% agreed in the November truce with Xi.

Numerous products are exempted, including oil and gas, fertilizer, certain foodstuffs, aircraft and parts, critical minerals, and goods already subject to Section 232 tariffs (autos, steel, aluminum, copper). Two US small businesses — Burlap and Barrel (spices) and Collective Horology (watches) — filed suit on Friday challenging the tariffs as exceeding Section 301 authority. An outside budget analysis found the new duties replace less than 60% of the revenue lost when the Supreme Court struck down the prior global tariff.

A second Section 301 investigation into 'excess capacity' targeting 16 trading partners — including the EU, China, India, Japan, and Switzerland — is still pending and would add further tariffs on top.
sections.whyItMatters: The tariff wall never came down. Section 301 has survived court challenges before, giving these duties stronger legal footing than the struck-down emergency tariffs. The forced-labor framing also makes them politically harder to oppose, but the revenue gap and the lawsuit signal friction ahead.

sections.heading: Houthis Strike Saudi Tankers, Opening a Second Chokepoint as Brent Crosses $100
sections.body:
Yemen's Houthi rebels struck two Saudi oil tankers — the Encelia and the Layla — in the Red Sea early Thursday, following through on their Monday declaration of a naval blockade against Saudi-linked shipping. Brent crude futures surged past $100 a barrel for the first time since May, before retreating slightly to near $99 on Friday as reports emerged of possible Pakistan-Iran talks.

The Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea — just 19 miles wide — has been the critical alternative route for Saudi oil since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in March. Saudi Arabia has been pumping roughly 3.5 million barrels per day through its Yanbu pipeline to the Red Sea. If the Houthi blockade closes Bab el-Mandeb, rerouting via the Cape of Good Hope would add 2,700 miles and an estimated $5 million in freight costs per vessel, excluding fuel and insurance. The Suez Canal cannot handle Very Large Crude Carriers.

According to the International Energy Research Institute, a full closure of Bab el-Mandeb could reduce global oil supply by an additional 7% on top of the roughly 10% reduction already caused by the Hormuz closure. The IMF has warned that oil market buffers are running low. War risk insurance premiums for Saudi ports have risen to around 0.75% of ship value, from 0.3% before the blockade announcement.

President Trump warned that 'major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran' if the blockade continues, calling the Houthis a 'surrogate and/or proxy of Iran.' He also told Axios he is 'considering a massive attack, bigger than ever before' on Iran.
sections.whyItMatters: The Middle East now has two simultaneous chokepoints. The Red Sea was the bypass route keeping Saudi exports flowing — its closure means no easy way out for Gulf oil. Each additional month of disruption adds roughly $10-15 to Brent, according to Barclays and JPMorgan estimates.

sections.heading: US Strikes Iran for 13th Night as Trump Weighs Escalation
sections.body:
US missiles struck targets across Iran for the 13th consecutive night on Thursday, reaching as far as Iran's Caspian coast, according to Reuters and AP reporting. The US military said it targeted drone facilities, coastal surveillance sites, and other military infrastructure. Trump met with his cabinet on Thursday to discuss whether to intensify strikes, days before a planned meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu.

Iran rejected Trump's threats as 'bullying and coercion,' while the US military also fired on a merchant vessel attempting to breach its blockade of Iranian ports. At least seven explosions were reported near a US-hosted military base in Irbil, northern Iraq. The UN warned against further escalation, noting the risks to global shipping from the widening conflict.

According to USNI News, Hormuz transits remain at low levels, with the US blockade of Iranian ports continuing alongside Iran's own closure of the strait. A Malaysian vessel was cleared through the Red Sea and is expected in Melaka in early August, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim confirmed.
sections.whyItMatters: The conflict is now in a grinding phase — daily strikes, no clear off-ramp. Trump's cabinet meeting on escalation levels and the upcoming Netanyahu visit suggest a decision point on whether to broaden the campaign or pursue negotiations.

sections.heading: Fed Hike Odds Hit One-in-Three as Jobs Market Stays Red-Hot
sections.body:
Weekly US jobless claims fell to a seasonally adjusted 187,000 for the week ending July 18 — the lowest reading since 1969 — pushing the probability of a Fed rate hike at the July 29-30 meeting past one-in-three, according to market pricing. CNBC published an opinion piece titled 'Why the Federal Reserve Should Hike Rates Next Week,' arguing that 'the potential cost of an energy-driven surge in prices outweighs the cost of a modest preemptive hike.'

The Fed is widely expected to hold rates steady at next week's meeting, but the combination of oil above $100, a tight labor market, and new tariffs has reshaped the debate. Bond yields have edged higher as tariff and energy inflation risks compound. Mortgage rates rose in tandem, with analysts at HSBC predicting higher rates 'until at least September' due to the Iran conflict's impact on oil prices.

The dollar hit a 40-year high against the yen earlier this week, reflecting the divergent monetary policy paths between a hawkish-leaning Fed and a Bank of Japan that only recently reached 1%. Emerging market currencies are also under pressure: the ringgit is expected to trade at RM4.08-4.10 next week on Fed and oil jitters.
sections.whyItMatters: The Fed is caught between a labor market that screams 'no cut' and a geopolitical shock that could push inflation higher. Even a hold with hawkish forward guidance would tighten financial conditions. The question is whether the energy and tariff shocks are transient or persistent enough to warrant action.

sections.heading: EU's 21st Sanctions Package Hits Russian Finance Hard — 94 Banks, Crypto Networks, Shadow Fleet
sections.body:
The EU adopted its 21st sanctions package against Russia on July 23 — its largest in four years — with 218 new designations (170 entities, 48 individuals) bringing total listings to nearly 3,000. The package targets the financial system directly: full asset-freeze sanctions on 94 Russian financial institutions (including state-owned Rosselkhozbank, Wildberries Bank, and Ozon Bank), SWIFT disconnection for 33 additional Russian banks, and four third-country banks in Mongolia, Kyrgyzstan, and Indian subsidiaries.

The crypto dimension is significant. The EU extended transaction bans to 14 third-country crypto platforms in Georgia, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Belarus, and the UAE, and designated four entities linked to the A7 cross-border payment network — whose rouble-pegged A7A5 stablecoin has processed nearly $120 billion, according to Chainalysis. The package also created a new legal basis to ban all transactions between EU operators and any crypto provider used by Russia in a third country — a tool that could effectively cut off entire jurisdictions from EU crypto infrastructure.

On energy, the EU froze the Russian oil price cap at $44.10/barrel for 12 months, preventing an automatic increase to around $58.50. The shadow fleet was hit with 41 new vessel listings (total now over 670), and a new rule enables EU countries to confiscate and sell cargoes carried by detained shadow-fleet vessels. The Russian LNG import ban takes effect January 1, 2027, with a one-year exemption for existing contracts capped at 2025 volumes.

The package came just three days after Russia's State Duma passed its first comprehensive crypto regulation framework, effective September 1.
sections.whyItMatters: The EU is no longer just sanctioning Russian entities — it's building infrastructure to cut off entire third-country crypto ecosystems. The A7 network designation and the new third-country ban power are escalations that go beyond targeting Russia to reshaping how crypto operates globally as a sanctions-evasion tool.

sections.heading: Emerging Market Bonds Hit as Tariffs Add to War Shock
sections.body:
Pakistan's international sovereign bonds slid 0.5% on Friday after the new forced-labor tariffs were imposed, and Sri Lanka and Indonesia bonds also fell, according to Reuters. The combination of elevated oil prices from the Middle East conflict and new trade barriers is compounding pressure on import-dependent emerging markets already running large current account deficits.

Indian equity markets reflected the strain: the BSE Sensex and NSE Nifty50 both fell roughly 2% this week as Brent crude hit $100/barrel. China has accelerated purchases of Russian ESPO crude as Middle East supply risks escalate, according to reports, seeking to lock in discounted Russian barrels as a hedge against further disruption.

The week's major indexes closed lower for a second straight week, with the Nasdaq dropping on chip stock weakness while energy and resource stocks outperformed. Barclays sees upside risks to its Brent price forecast depending on how long the Hormuz impasse lasts, while JPMorgan noted that oil has been 'remarkably restrained' given the scale of disruptions — suggesting further upside is possible if the conflict widens.
sections.whyItMatters: The dual shock of oil and tariffs is hitting the countries least able to absorb it. Pakistan, Sri Lanka, and Indonesia are all IMF program countries — new tariff costs on top of energy inflation strain their adjustment programs and could force policy reversals.

sections.heading: Senate Russia Sanctions Bill Snarled by Tariff Dispute
sections.body:
A bipartisan Russia sanctions bill championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham has become snarled in a dispute over expanding presidential tariff authority, the New York Times reported on Thursday. The bill, which would impose sweeping secondary sanctions on countries doing business with Russia, has broad support — but negotiations have deadlocked over a provision that would expand the president's power to impose tariffs on countries that don't comply with the sanctions regime.

The dispute reflects the broader tension in Congress between those who want maximum economic pressure on Russia and those wary of giving the executive branch even broader trade powers — particularly given Trump's aggressive use of tariff authority. The bill remains stalled with no clear timeline for resolution.
sections.whyItMatters: The legislative vehicle for the most aggressive Russia sanctions in years is stuck not on Russia policy, but on how much tariff power the president should have. In the current environment, that debate is far more contentious than the sanctions themselves.

bottomLine: Trump's forced-labor tariffs seamlessly replaced the expiring 10% global duty, keeping the tariff wall intact on 99.4% of US imports with stronger legal footing — but covering only 60% of the lost revenue and drawing immediate legal challenge. Meanwhile, Brent crude crossed $100 after Houthi strikes on Saudi tankers opened a second chokepoint at Bab el-Mandeb, compounding the Hormuz closure that has already cut global supply by 10%. The dual shock of oil and tariffs is now hitting emerging markets (Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Indonesia bonds all fell) and pushing Fed hike odds past one-in-three ahead of next week's FOMC meeting. The EU, for its part, delivered its largest Russia sanctions package in four years — targeting 94 banks, 14 crypto platforms, and the A7 stablecoin network that has processed $120 billion in sanctions-evasion flows. The Middle East conflict shows no sign of de-escalation; Trump is weighing a 'massive' attack on Iran, and there is no clear off-ramp in sight.
sources: Reuters, CNBC, MSN, CoinDesk, USA Today, CSMonitor, Institute for Energy Research, USNI News, AP, NYT, Bloomberg, Arkansas Online, NewsBytes, Malay Mail, New Indian Express, Barclays, JPMorgan, Yahoo Finance, AOL/Reuters Factbox, IG Markets
